text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Rose v. RCMP,

2009 BCSC 1116

Date: 20090814

Docket:
S55166

Registry: Nanaimo

Between:

Jerry Douglas Rose Jr.

Plaintiff

And

Her Majesty the Queen and Her Loyal
Servants the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (on duty and off duty) in Right of
the Province of British Columbia, the Attorney General of British Columbia, the
City of Nanaimo, Microsoft Corporation, Microsoft Canada, Intel Corporation,
Telus Corporation, Google Inc., and General Dynamics – Itronix and Microsoft
Certified Professionals – Jeremy Dawson and Colon (Last known address 1750
Starling Road, Nanaimo British Columbia)

Defendants

And

Docket:
S55228

Registry: Nanaimo

Between:

Jerry Douglas Rose Jr.

Plaintiff

And:

Her Majesty the Queen and Her Loyal Servants the Royal Canadian
Mounted Police (on duty and off duty) in Right of the Province of British
Columbia, the Attorney General of British Columbia, the Solicitor General of
British Columbia, the City of Nanaimo, Microsoft Corporation, Microsoft Canada,
Intel Corporation, Google Inc., and General Dynamics Itronix and Microsoft
Certified Professionals; Jeremy Dawson and Colon (Last known address 1750
Starling Road, Nanaimo British Columbia)

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Halfyard

Reasons for Judgment

Appearing on his own behalf in both
actions

Jerry Douglas Rose Jr.

Counsel for Her Majesty the Queen and the
Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Solicitor General of British Columbia

M.F. Volk

Counsel for Her Majesty the Queen in
Right of the Province of British Columbia

H. Gwillim

Counsel for Microsoft Corporation and
Microsoft Canada

J. Millbank

Counsel for Telus Corporation and Agent
for General Dynamics – Itronix

K. Gammon

Appearing on his own behalf in both
actions:

Colin McFadden

Place and Date of Hearing:

Nanaimo, B.C.

July 23, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

Nanaimo, B.C.

August 14, 2009

Introduction

[
1
]

In these two actions, the defendants Her Majesty
the Queen and Her Loyal Servants the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (On Duty and
Off Duty) in Right of the Province of British Columbia, The Solicitor General
of British Columbia, Telus Corporation and General Dynamics – Itronix have made
applications for orders striking out the statements of claim and dismissing the
proceedings.  The applications are made pursuant to Rule 19(24).

[
2
]

The Solicitor General of British Columbia also
applies for an order to remove his name from the style of cause on the ground
that he has not been made a proper party to action S55166.  The ground of this
application is that the plaintiff added the Solicitor General of British
Columbia as a party, without obtaining leave of the court, as required by Rule
15(5)(a).

[
3
]

The plaintiff conceded that he had added the
Solicitor General of British Columbia as a party when he filed amended
pleadings on March 20, 2009.  He did this without court order.  Accordingly,
the Solicitor General of British Columbia will be removed from the style of
cause and from paragraphs 25, 26 and 29 of the amended statement of claim.
References to “the Ministry of Public Safety” in paragraphs 25, 26, 27 and 29
will also be removed from the amended statement of claim.

[
4
]

At the outset of the hearing, the plaintiff
sought leave to remove five defendants as parties in both actions, namely, the
Attorney General of British Columbia, the City of Nanaimo, Microsoft
Corporation, Microsoft Canada and Intel Corporation.  In view of Rule 36, leave
of the court was not required.  I made an order that discontinuances would be
deemed to be filed as against those five defendants, in both actions.

[
5
]

Counsel for Microsoft Corporation and Microsoft
Canada submitted that the reference to “Microsoft Certified Professionals” in
the style of cause should be deleted, on the ground that it is not a legal
entity capable of being sued.  The plaintiff acknowledged that he used this
term only to describe the defendants Jeremy Dawson and Colin McFadden.  This
point was properly taken, and I order that Microsoft Certified Professionals be
deleted from the styles of cause in both actions.

[
6
]

Counsel for Her Majesty the Queen (and The Royal
Canadian Mounted Police) had also filed an application for dismissal under Rule
18(6).  Ms. Volk did not proceed with that application, and it was adjourned
generally.

[
7
]

The plaintiff has filed an application in which
he seeks final judgment on liability as against the defendants General Dynamics
– Itronix and Google Inc., on the ground that they have failed to file and
deliver an appearance or a statement of defence in compliance with the Rules of
Court.  I adjourned that application generally, pending my decision on the
applications under Rule 19(24).

The Ground of the Applications

[
8
]

The applicants rely on all four grounds stated
in Rule 19(24).  That Rule reads as follows:

(24)  At any stage of a proceeding the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses no reasonable claim or
defence as the case may be,

(b) it is unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may prejudice, embarrass or delay
the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d) it is otherwise an abuse of the
process of the court,

and the court
may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may
order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

The Actions

[
9
]

Action number S55166 was commenced on December 9, 2008.
On March 20, 2009, the plaintiff filed an amended statement of
claim.  Reading the amended statement of claim, (which contains 29 numbered
paragraphs), in the context of the plaintiff’s affidavit sworn July 21, 2009
and his submissions made during the hearing, enables me to summarize what the
plaintiff is attempting to say in his pleadings.  In substance, the plaintiff
alleges (or could, by amendment allege) as follows:

a.

He was subjected to brain surgery without his
knowledge or consent, in or about 2003;

b.

In this surgery, an electronic micro chip was
implanted in the left hemisphere of the plaintiff’s brain, and a radio
frequency chip was implanted at the top of the plaintiff’s neck, behind his
right ear;

c.

This surgery was performed by persons unknown,
but was done under the direction of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police;

d.

The electronic devices implanted in the
plaintiff’s brain and neck make it possible for an outside observer using
advanced communication technologies to monitor the content of the plaintiff’s
thought processes, and to induce particular thoughts in the plaintiff’s mind,
without the plaintiff being aware of it;

e.

The RCMP has been continuously conducting
surveillance of the plaintiff’s thought processes, and has from time to time
planted thoughts and impulses in the plaintiff’s mind;

f.

For the most part, the plaintiff has been
subjected to these invasive procedures as part of experimental research being
done by the RCMP, presumably to learn how to monitor and control the thought
processes of criminals;

g.

Telus Corporation has full knowledge of
everything that has been done to the plaintiff by the RCMP, has partaken in the
development of the advanced communications technology being used against the plaintiff,
and has been engaged in a conspiracy with the RCMP to further the experiments
being conducted on the plaintiff;

h.

The RCMP and Google Inc. are engaged in a
conspiracy somewhat similar to that between the RCMP and Telus;

i.

Jeremy Dawson and Colin McFadden, through
employment or consultation with Microsoft, have been involved in the
development and operation of the surveillance and control of the plaintiff’s
thought processes, by means of the advanced communications technologies;

j.

The wrongful conduct of the RCMP against the
plaintiff has been malicious;

k.

The described wrongful conduct has caused
physical and psychological harm to the plaintiff, which will be permanent, and
has also caused loss of income, personal possessions and opportunity for career
advancement;

l.

The physical injuries caused by the wrongful
conduct of the RCMP (which amounts to assault and torture) includes laser burns
to the cornea of his eye, nerve damage to his face and ear and severe muscle
cramps, all of which injuries have caused severe pain to the plaintiff;

m.

The Province of British Columbia (Her Majesty the Queen) has
committed negligence causing harm to the plaintiff and to the general public,
by facilitating the use of advanced communications technology by the RCMP for
improper purposes;

n.

The RCMP has trespassed upon the plaintiff’s
land in the course of its wrongdoing against the plaintiff;

o.

During these trespasses, which took place around
the time of the brain surgery on the plaintiff and also in May 2008, the RCMP
killed two of the plaintiff’s dogs and seriously injured another of the
plaintiff’s dogs;

p.

As part of the illegal surveillance, the RCMP
monitored the plaintiff and his ex-common-law wife while they were engaging in
sexual activities;

q.

If the plaintiff succeeds in proving liability
against one or more of the defendants, he claims damages (including punitive
damages) in the amount of $2,000,000,000.

[
10
]

The plaintiff commenced action No. S55228 on
December 17, 2008.  On March 20, 2009, he filed an amended
statement of claim.  From this pleading, read together with the amended
statement of claim in action No. S55166 (and in light of the submissions made
by the plaintiff at the hearing), I interpret the substance of the main
allegations in this action to be as follows:

a.

The plaintiff has made repeated demands upon the
RCMP that they cease and desist from the wrongful conduct which he has outlined
in his pleadings in action No. S55166;

b.

The plaintiff has made these demands to the
RCMP, between June 27, 2009 (I take this to mean 2008) and the
present time (i.e. March 20, 2009), but the RCMP has ignored the
plaintiff’s demands and has continued the wrongful conduct;

c.

The RCMP has downloaded the plaintiff’s entire
brain function, as well as his long-term memories and short-term memories, to a
database which it controls and which it uses to manipulate the plaintiff’s
brain function without his knowledge or consent;

d.

This covert and illegal surveillance
communication system is used by the RCMP to monitor and control the brain
functions of individuals who live in various parts of Vancouver Island,
including Sannich, Nanaimo, Cedar and the Vancouver Island Regional
Correctional Centre;

e.

The RCMP and persons trained by Microsoft have
induced false and slanderous beliefs about the plaintiff, in the minds of some
members of the RCMP and other people, by means of the illegal communications
system;

f.

The RCMP committed wrongful acts against the
plaintiff on five occasions when he attended at Nanaimo Regional General
Hospital for treatment which wrongful acts included a serious assault and
arrest of the plaintiff, and subjecting the plaintiff to brain-function
manipulation by means of the illegal monitoring and control of the plaintiff’s
thought processes (using the illegal communications system);

g.

The constant harassment by the RCMP has caused
physical and psychological injury, and financial loss to the plaintiff (similar
to the adverse effects alleged in the second action);

h.

The harassment by the RCMP has interfered with
the plaintiff obtaining necessary treatment for Hepatitis C;

i.

The conduct of the RCMP has violated the
plaintiff’s rights as guaranteed by the
Charter of Rights
(
ss. 12
and
15
) by
subjecting him to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment and by failing to
treat the plaintiff as being equal under the law;

j.

The plaintiff claims damages (including punitive
damages) in the specific amount of $1,425,000,008.88.  (In court, I understood
Mr. Rose to say that he calculated damages by charging between 1.2 cents and
1.6 cents for each of his neurons that were adversely affected by the RCMP).

[
11
]

The amended statement of claim in action No.
S55228 contains 11 paragraphs.  Paragraphs 7 and 8 are almost identical to
paragraphs 21 and 28 of the statement of claim in action No. S55166.  The
unnumbered paragraph which appears just before the prayer for relief is
essentially the same as the paragraph which immediately precedes the prayer for
relief in action No. S55166.

[
12
]

The plaintiff has named the same defendants in
both of these actions, except that in action No. S55228, Telus Corporation is
not sued and is not mentioned in the pleadings.

Do the amended statements of claim in
either of these two actions disclose a reasonable claim?

[
13
]

No evidence is admissible on this part of the
application:  See Rule 19(27).

[
14
]

The test for determining whether a statement of
claim fails to disclose any reasonable claim requires the applicant to persuade
the court that, assuming that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can
be proved, is it plain and obvious that the action is certain to fail?  See
Carey
Canada Inc. v. Hunt,

1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at 980.  I consider this test to mean
that an applicant must show that there is no reasonable possibility that any of
the claims will succeed if a trial is held.

[
15
]

One of the main submissions made by counsel for
the applicants was that in a previous action (S53706) brought by the plaintiff
against multiple defendants including the RCMP, Microsoft, Google, Telus and
the Province of British Columbia, this court decided that substantially similar
claims failed to disclose any reasonable claim against any of the defendants.
See
Jerry Rose Jr. V. The University of British Columbia et al.

2008
BCSC 1661
(A.F. Wilson J.).  It was pointed out that
Mr. Justice Wilson struck out the statement of claim and dismissed
the action as against all defendants, on each of the grounds set out in Rule
19(24)(a), (b) and (c).  Consequently, it was argued that the present
proceedings (i.e., both of the two new actions) are
res judicata
,
vexatious and an abuse of the process of the court.  Numerous other arguments
were made, but to my mind these are the points on which these applications
turn.  These issues require me to consider the pleadings and the reasons for
judgment of Mr. Justice Wilson in the previous action (“the first
action”).

[
16
]

Mr. Rose cited the judgment of Mr. Justice
Williams in
Ross v. British Columbia (Public Safety)

2009 BCSC 930
, in
support of his submissions in opposition to the present applications.  In that
case, the defendants were seeking summary judgment dismissing the plaintiff’s
action pursuant to Rule 18(6).  The plaintiff was making allegations that were
somewhat similar to those being made by Mr. Rose in his law suits.  Williams J.
decided that the defendants had failed to prove that there was no merit to the
plaintiff’s claim, and dismissed the application.  The court found insufficient
the affidavit evidence given by Staff Sergeant Kjenhus, the officer in charge
of the Hope Detachment (see paragraphs 13 and 27 of the reasons for judgment).

[
17
]

Counsel for the present applicants argued that
the
Ross
case was distinguishable from the present cases, in that the
test under Rule 18(6) is different from that under Rule 19(24), and that the
affidavit evidence given by RCMP Superintendent Jeff Lott in this case goes
much further than the evidence before Mr. Justice Williams.

[
18
]

It seems to me that the test under Rule 18(6) is
similar to that required of an applicant under Rule 19(24)(a).  Williams J.
stated (at para 26) that the test under Rule 18(6) requires a defendant to show
that the plaintiff is bound to lose.  However, I agree with counsel that the
evidence of Superintendant Lott is superior to the evidence that was before Mr.
Justice Williams, on the issue of the knowledge of the RCMP about the technologies
described by the plaintiff (but of course this evidence is not admissible on
the Rule 19(24)(a) issue).  In addition, Mr. Justice Williams was not asked to
assess the statement of claim on any ground in Rule 19(24).  Accordingly, while
the decision of Williams J. is of interest, I do not think it has any direct
bearing on the issues that I must decide.

[
19
]

As to Mr. Justice Wilson’s decision
that the pleadings failed to disclose any reasonable claim, paragraphs 6, 7, 8,
12 and 13 are of particular relevance.  As I read these reasons, Wilson J.
decided that the allegations made by the plaintiff were wild speculation and
were incapable of proof.  In doing so, he relied on the reasoning of Thackeray,
J.A. in
Young v. Borzoni

2007 BCCA 16
.  Central to Wilson J.’s decision
that the allegations were mere speculation was the fact that the allegations
were directed against all of the defendants but without stating when, where or
how the wrongful acts are alleged to have been committed or by whom.

[
20
]

Paragraph 14 of his reasons for judgment sets
out Mr. Justice Wilson’s reasoning on the issues under Rule 19(24)(b) and (c).
He described the pleadings as being “without substance, groundless, fanciful”
and which would “waste the time of the court.”  Wilson J. also stated that
the pleadings were “prolix, including irrelevant facts and argument and are
constructed in such a way to make it virtually impossible for each of the
individual defendants to answer the allegations made against that particular
defendant, apart from by a general denial.”  Wilson J. again mentioned the
failure to “distinguish between the various defendants insofar as the various
tortuous acts are alleged, nor provide particulars of when, where and how those
acts are alleged to have occurred.”  Finally, Wilson J. noted that there
was no connection between the allegations and the relief being claimed by the
plaintiff.

[
21
]

Mr. Justice Wilson attached the
statement of claim in that action as an appendix to the reasons for judgment.
I have studied that pleading in comparison with the amended statement of claim
in action No. S55166 (“the second action”).  In my opinion, all of the main
allegations in the second action are substantially the same as those that were
made in the first action.  In the second action, paragraphs 10, 11, 12, 13, 14,
17, 19, 20 and 24 have corresponding similar paragraphs in the statement of
claim in the first action, but in the second action, the term “the defendants”
has been changed to “the RCMP” in the mentioned paragraphs.

[
22
]

In the second action, paragraph 6 alleges that
the RCMP, Jeremy Dawson and Colin McFadden have violated various rights of the
plaintiff “in the pursuit of covering up their involvement in the facilitation
and operation of the brain computer interface brain to brain network
surveillance system – see Appendix I.”  (Appendix I was attached to the
original statement of claim filed on December 9, 2008, and it contained
excerpts from various statutes and a 3-page document dated April 4 and 5, 2008,
which is entitled “Invasive BCI and neuro-technology.”)

[
23
]

In the second action, paragraphs 17, 21 and 25
of the statement of claim in the first action have been omitted.  The prayer
for relief in the first action included a claim for delivery of 7 motor
vehicles, but that claim was not made in the second action.

[
24
]

Although not all of the entities named as
defendants in the first action have been sued in the second action, and there
are some additional defendants named in the second action (Intel Corporation,
General Dynamics-Itronix, Jeremy Dawson and Colin McFadden), there is again a
large group of defendants being sued.

[
25
]

As I see it, the nature of the alleged wrongful
acts and the alleged consequences of those wrongful acts are almost identical
in both the first action and the second action.  Paragraphs 23 through 29 of
the amended statement of claim in the second action are new, in the sense that
they do not appear in the statement of claim in the first action, and so they
require consideration.

[
26
]

In paragraph 23, the plaintiff alleges that
Telus Corporation has full knowledge about the wrongful actions of the RCMP
against the plaintiff, and has been involved in that wrongful conduct by way of
“an ongoing relationship” with the RCMP.  Paragraph 24 describes the
relationship between Telus Corporation and the RCMP as being a conspiracy
(presumably to injure the plaintiff).

[
27
]

In paragraphs 25 and 26, the plaintiff alleges
that the Province of British Columbia was negligent in allowing the RCMP to
gain access to the plaintiff’s “neuro-synaptic activity by way of the BCI-BTB
network surveillance communications system” (which access was also facilitated
by the Solicitor General of British Columbia, the Ministry of Public Safety and
the Royal Canadian Mounted Police).

[
28
]

In paragraph 26, the plaintiff alleges that the
Province of British Columbia was “negligent in their duty to insure public
safety” (it is implied that this is the same negligence as that committed in
respect of the plaintiff), and that there was involvement in this negligence by
the Solicitor General of British Columbia and the Ministry of Public Safety.

[
29
]

Paragraph 27 alleges that the RCMP and the
Ministry of Public Safety illegally monitored the plaintiff’s brain functions
and harassed him on a daily basis, while he was in custody at the Vancouver
Island Regional Correctional Centre.  In paragraph 28, the plaintiff alleges
“an ongoing relationship” between Google Inc. and the RCMP with respect to some
of the wrongful actions committed by the RCMP against the plaintiff.

[
30
]

Paragraph 29 alleges that various locations in
and around the City of Nanaimo are areas in which the RCMP (together with the
Solicitor General of British Columbia and the Ministry of Public Safety) are
able to practice their wrongful actions on the plaintiff and other persons.

[
31
]

I do not think the addition of paragraphs 23 to
29, or any of the other differences between the first action and the second
action, are of sufficient importance to make the judgment of
Mr. Justice Wilson in the first action inapplicable to the second
action.

[
32
]

Mr. Justice Wilson dismissed the plaintiff’s
first action on three separate and independent grounds, the first being that
the statement of claim failed to disclose any reasonable claim.  That
conclusion rested on his finding that the allegations were “wild speculation,”
and therefore were incapable of proof.  It is true that Wilson J. relied
on the fact that most of the allegations were made against all of the defendants,
without distinguishing and particularizing the acts of each defendant
separately, in concluding that the allegations constituted “wild speculation.”
In the second action, the plaintiff has identified the RCMP as being the main
wrongdoer.  However, there are allegations that many of the other defendants
are also involved in the wrongdoing, which implies that they are engaged in a
conspiracy with the RCMP.  Accordingly, I do not think that this difference
between the two statements of claim is of much significance.  The fundamental
allegation is the same in both actions, namely, that the RCMP, assisted by the
other defendants, and/or using systems created by the other defendants, have
controlled and manipulated the plaintiff’s brain functions and thought processes
without his knowledge and consent.  In my opinion, the main allegations in the
first action and the second action either consist of or relate to the same
subject matter.

[
33
]

The judgment of Mr. Justice Wilson has not
been appealed.  In my opinion, the decision of Mr. Justice  Wilson
that the pleadings in the first action failed to disclose any reasonable claim
applies as an estoppel to the second action, at least with respect to all
defendants who are common to both proceedings (which include the present
applicants).  In his preliminary application for leave to discontinue, the
plaintiff conceded that there was no cause of action as against Microsoft
Corporation and Microsoft Canada.  It would seem to follow that there could be
no cause of action against the “Microsoft-certified Professionals”, namely
Jeremy Dawson and Colin McFadden.  In any event, I find that no cause of action
is pleaded against either of these two men.  With respect to the other present
defendant that was not sued in the first action, i.e., General
Dynamics-Itronix, I note that it is alleged in para 21, in effect, that this
defendant sold computers to the RCMP that were used in their police vehicles.
I would invoke the inherent jurisdiction of the court and decide that the
pleadings disclose no reasonable claim as against that defendant either.

[
34
]

In the result, pursuant to Rule 19(24)(a), the
statement of claim in the second action (unless it is amendable) should be
struck out as against all of the defendants remaining after the discontinuances
entered as to the Attorney General of British Columbia, the City of Nanaimo,
Microsoft Corporation, Microsoft Canada and Intel Corporation.

Rule 19(24)(b):  Is the second action
vexatious?

[
35
]

The rule which in my view applies here was
stated by Madam Justice Garson in
Dempsey  v. Envision
Credit Union et al.
2006 BCSC 750
at paragraph
10
in this way:

. . .Parties may not bring forward in a
subsequent action points related to the subject matter of previous litigation
that the parties, exercising reasonable diligence, might have been able to
bring forward. . . .

See also
Freshway Specialty Foods v. Map
Produce LLC

2005 BCSC 1485
at paragraphs
50
, 53 and 54;
Perley v. Sypher

1990 Can. III 4005 (NBCA);
Wayneroy Holdings v. British Columbia (Minister
of Environment, Lands and Parks)

2002 BCSC 1510
at paragraphs
19 to 21
;
Budgell
v. Oppal

2007 BCSC 991
at paragraph
23
.

[
36
]

One of the arguments made by the applicants was
that these actions were vexatious and an abuse of process, because the
plaintiff was using the court process for an improper purpose.  I reject that
submission.  In my judgment, Mr. Rose honestly believes in the truth of the
allegations that he is making and that he is not pursuing this litigation for
any improper purpose.  However, it is my opinion that the plaintiff is, in the
second action, raising issues that were raised and decided against him in the
first action.  To the extent that the second action may differ slightly from
the first action, any such different issues could have (and should have) been
raised in the first action.  In my view, the bringing of the second action
constitutes an abuse of the court process, notwithstanding that such abuse is
unintentional.  This process could also be characterized as a collateral attack
on the order made by Mr. Justice Wilson.

[
37
]

In my view, the pleadings in the second action
should be struck out on the ground that they are vexatious and an abuse of the
process of the court, contrary to Rule 19(24)(b).

Rule
19(24)(c): Are the pleadings in the second action embarrassing?

[
38
]

Mr. Justice Wilson also decided that the
statement of claim in the first action should be struck out on the ground in
Rule 19(24)(c).  I agree with his finding that the pleadings in the first
action were embarrassing.  A definition of embarrassing pleadings was given by
Mr. Justice Romilly as being “when pleadings are so confusing that it is
difficult to understand what is being pleaded.”  See
Citizens for Foreign
Aid Reform inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999)
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. 4th 266 at
paragraph
47
.  A similar definition was given by Madam Justice Allan in
McNutt
v. Canada (Attorney General)
2004 BCSC 1113
, at paragraph
41
.
I
think that description applies to many of the statements made in the statement
of claim in both the first action and the second action.  In my view, that
would constitute a further ground for striking out much of the statement of
claim in the second action.

The Third
Action

[
39
]

I have already summarized the allegations made
in the third action.  In my opinion, that action is founded on the same alleged
facts as the first action and the second action.  It seems to me that all of
the issues raised in the third action are closely related to the subject matter
of the first and second actions.  Those points properly belonged to the same
subject of litigation, and in my view they should have been raised in the
earlier proceedings.  Without subjecting the third action to the same detailed
analysis as I have done with respect to the second action, my opinion is that
the plaintiff’s pleadings in the third action should be struck out on this
obvious ground as against all of the named defendants.

Can any of the
defects in the pleadings be cured by amendment?

[
40
]

Mr. Justice Wilson held (at par. 18) that the
statement of claim in the first action was “incapable of amendment.”  In the
present case, Mr. Rose filed affidavit evidence which may be considered on the
issue of whether leave to amend should be granted.  His affidavit sworn
July 21, 2009 contains (among others) assertions which I would
paraphrase in this way:

a.

A CAT scan performed on April 29, 2009
shows that a foreign object is located on the left hemisphere of his brain,
which has the shape of an “injectable microchip”;

b.

He had an MRI scan performed on
May 15, 2009, which he believes will corroborate the CAT scan
findings;

c.

He has had several cranial x-rays done in 2008
and 2009, which he says will provide further corroborating evidence for the
existence of a microchip shaped device in his brain;

d.

He had x-rays of his cervical spine taken on
July 2, 2009 which he says show that he has a radio frequency chip implanted in
his spine behind his right ear;

e.

He is knowledgeable concerning many
technologies, including microchip technology and human brain functions;

f.

His former common law wife can give evidence
that she has an injection mark at the back of her neck, and can testify about
relevant events between 2003 and 2006;

g.

He intends to have testing done on his brain,
which he believes will confirm that microwave radio frequency is emanating from
the cortex of his brain; and

h.

He can produce documents which will show an
ongoing relationship between Telus and the RCMP.

[
41
]

Ms. Volk submitted that the evidence presented
by Mr. Rose consisted mainly of his own personal opinions, and could not prove
that the alleged communications technology exists, or that such technology has
been used by the RCMP against him, or that he has microchips in his brain or
cervical spine.  Counsel emphasized the absence of any expert evidence.  It
seems implicit in this argument that no purpose could be served by granting
leave to amend, because the plaintiff will never be able to prove his
allegations.  Ms. Volk points to the affidavit of RCMP superintendent Jeff Lott
sworn June 17, 2009.  She submits (and I agree) that Superintendent Lott’s
evidence establishes:

a.

that he has no knowledge of any of the technologies and systems
described in the statements of claim;

b.

that none of the described technologies and systems are used by the
RCMP or are available to the RCMP; and

c.

that the RCMP has not engaged in any of the wrongful conduct which
Mr. Rose claims they have committed against him.

[
42
]

It is true that the court will not order
amendments which could serve no useful purpose.  See
Young v. Lort

2007
BCSC 1152
, at para.
33
.

[
43
]

If it follows logically from Mr. Justice
Wilson’s decision in the first action that the plaintiff’s allegations in the
second and third actions are incapable of proof, then it would be useless to
grant leave to amend.  But in my opinion, there is a further ground for
refusing amendment, namely, that these two actions raise issues that are
similar and closely connected to issues that were raised and decided against
the plaintiff in the first action.  I would not grant leave to amend.

[
44
]

For these reasons, I have concluded that Action
No. S55166 and Action No. S55228 should be dismissed as against all of the
defendants who remain as parties following the discontinuances.  It is so
ordered.

The Fourth
Action

[
45
]

On June 24, 2009, Mr. Rose filed a notice of
claim in the Small Claims Division of the Provincial Court of British Columbia,
at Nanaimo.  The named defendants were Her Majesty the Queen in right of the
Province of British Columbia (together with her servants the Royal Canadian
Mounted Police) the Solicitor General of British Columbia, the Nanaimo
Provincial Court Sheriff’s Department and the Attorney General of British
Columbia.

[
46
]

In this Small Claims Court action, Mr. Rose
makes confusing allegations which I interpret to be along the following lines:

a.

He injured his right hand in a physical altercation with sheriff’s
officers at the Nanaimo Court House, on a date which was not specified;

b.

The injury was caused by the negligence of the Sheriff’s Department
in failing to provide adequate escort officers so as to physically control Mr.
Rose;

c.

It was necessary to control Mr. Rose’s physical movements, because
the RCMP manipulated his brain functions and caused him to become aggressive.
(In court, Mr. Rose stated that this manipulation caused him to punch a wall in
the courthouse at Nanaimo, in about July 2008.)

d.

The injury to Mr. Rose’s right hand was aggravated by a sheriff’s
officer at the Vancouver Island Regional Correctional Centre where he was being
held in custody and was required to make a court appearance by video
conferencing.

e.

The sheriff’s officer at the Correctional Centre forcibly grabbed
Mr. Rose’s injured right hand, lifted him up off the ground, and then held his
hand and arm up behind his back while escorting him a distance of about 100
feet, when the sheriff’s officer knew or ought to have known that Mr. Rose’s
right hand was injured.

f.

On May 25, 2008, (possibly 2009?) at the RCMP
station building at Nanaimo, Mr. Rose re-injured his right hand and cut his
right hand, as a result of the negligence of the RCMP.

g.

The said injury was caused while the plaintiff was opening the door
latch to go outside the police building and was due to a defective door latch
mechanism on the inside door handle.

h.

The RCMP knew or ought to have known that the door handle and
door-latch mechanism was defective and dangerous to use by persons who were
exiting the building.

i.

Mr. Rose is claiming compensatory damages of
$25,000 for the injuries to his right hand, and the effects of those injuries.

[
47
]

Although the Provincial Court file was
transferred to this court for the purpose of the hearing of the present
applications, it was not made the subject of any submissions advanced at the
hearing.  Mr. Gwillim, on behalf of the Provincial Crown, had filed an
application under s.18 of the
Supreme Court Act
, seeking to have Mr.
Rose declared a vexatious litigant, but that application was adjourned
generally.  I presume that the Small Claims court file was brought to this
court, in connection with that application.  As a consequence, I do not intend
to make any further reference to the fourth action.

The plaintiff’s application for default judgment

[
48
]

As mentioned, I postponed the plaintiff’s
application for default judgment against the defendants Google Inc. and General
Dynamics- Itronix (the grounds of the application were failure to file and

]
